extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, epistemology, and foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria about what counts as scientific knowledge and legitimate mathematical method — e.g., the role of perception vs. demonstration, the structure of concepts, and the proper form of mathematical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of concept-spheres (law of homogeneity and specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A science shall not be constituted by a general concept and an indefinite multiplicity immediately under it; knowledge shall descend by degrees from the general to the particular, through intermediate concepts and divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific completeness requires the faculty of subordinating the concept-spheres according to their different determinations so that knowledge is organised from the general to the particular (satisfying equally the law of homogeneity and that of specification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic form over mere certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The special characteristic of science does not lie in certainty but in the systematic form of knowledge, based on the gradual descent from the general to the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the perverted opinion that scientific character consists in greater certainty; science aims to facilitate rational knowledge by its form and enable completeness, not simply to maximize certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for direct perception-based judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments created directly out of perception, and founded upon it rather than on any demonstrations, are to science what the sun is to the world; immediate evidence is to be preferred to demonstrated truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every demonstration ultimately rests upon undemonstrated truth (perception); when direct evidence is available it should be used rather than syllogistic demonstration, which is only a makeshift when perception is too remote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as the source and foundation of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception, partly pure a priori (basis of mathematics) and partly empirical a posteriori (basis of other sciences), is the source of all truth and the foundation of all science (logic excepted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All primal evidence is perception—either empirical or founded upon a priori perception of conditions of possible experience—and thus science must connect to perception to attain absolute truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty of judgment as mediator and criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty of judgment consists in the power of rightly and accurately carrying over into abstract consciousness what is known in perception; it mediates between understanding and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only extraordinary strength of judgment can advance science; deficiency in judgment (silliness) is failing to grasp relative differences or identities of concepts. Judgment should generate primary propositions from perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration requires undemonstrated premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Every demonstration requires an undemonstrated truth which ultimately supports it; the old mistake is to think only what has been demonstrated is absolutely true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that proofs/syllogisms presuppose primary, undemonstrated insights; demonstrations are useful mainly for dispute and exposition, not as ultimate foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogisms: formally certain but materially precarious
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are perfectly certain as regards form, but very uncertain on account of their matter, the concepts, because concept-spheres are often vague and intersecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of overreliance on purely logical deduction: ambiguous or overlapping concepts can produce paralogisms and sophisms; place higher trust in immediate evidence where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical evidence must rest on a priori perception (intuition of space/time)
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence of mathematics rests essentially not upon demonstration but upon immediate perception: the a priori intuitions of space and time are the proper ground of mathematical necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical truths should be shown by appeal to the appropriate perceptual/a priori ground (intuition of space/time) so that knowledge of that something is and why it is coincide, rather than relying solely on abstract logical derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Euclidean (synthetic) method in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's method substitutes logical demonstration for the evidence of perception peculiar to mathematics, thereby separating knowledge that a thing is from knowledge why it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer analytical exposition that traces first insights back to perceptual grounds; Euclid's synthetic proofs are described as a 'perversity' that withholds inner connection and insight, often yielding only memorized results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical method preferred for exposition of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: An analysis of the process of thought in the first discovery of a geometrical truth provides empirical necessity and insight; the analytical method is desired instead of Euclid's synthetic method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, teach geometry and mathematics so that proofs convey why things are so (insight into the ground of being), even though complicated truths may pose difficulties for purely analytical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of sufficient reason as foundation of explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of sufficient reason expresses the universal form of all our ideas and knowledge; all explanation consists of reduction to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is itself incapable of further explanation and is equally certain in all its forms; explanations should show how propositions reduce to this principle (grounds and consequents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of induction in natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science proceeds largely from the consequent to the reason (induction); hypotheses are constructed and confirmed by many perceptions, but such induction never attains unconditional certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that empirical sciences rest on hypotheses and induction; arranged experiments that follow cause-to-effect provide greater certainty, but hypotheses themselves arise from inductive insight and may be revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic grounded in a priori counting/perception
rubrics_metrics.description: In arithmetic the truth is really allowed to come home to us through perception (counting), which is a priori in time; arithmetic and algebra are methods for abbreviating counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use perceptual/temporal intuition (counting) as the foundation for arithmetic truths; abstract symbols indicate operations but underlying certainty traces to this perception.
